By the definition of syntactic entailment, every open proof tree with premises \( T \) and conclusion \( \varphi \) under \( \mathcal{S} \) has a maximum segment where \( T \) can derive \( \varphi \) using the standard proof rules of the logical system. informal_statement: A logical system is satisfiable if and only if it is consistent.
informal_proof:
To establish that a system \( T \) is satisfiable if and only if it is consistent, we will demonstrate both directions of the equivalence.

**Forward Direction (\( \Rightarrow \)):**  
Assume \( T \) is satisfiable. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that \( T \) is not consistent. If \( T \) is inconsistent, it contains a contradiction, meaning both a statement and its negation are theorems of \( T \). However, since \( T \) is satisfiable, there exists at least one interpretation under which all statements in \( T \) are true. This interpretation would make both a statement and its negation true, which contradicts the definition of satisfiability. Therefore, our assumption that \( T \) is inconsistent must be false, implying that \( T \) is consistent.

**Backward Direction (\( \Leftarrow \)):**  
Assume \( T \) is consistent. By the Completeness Theorem, a consistent system has a model; that is, there exists an interpretation under which all statements in \( T \) are true. This directly implies that \( T \) is satisfiable.

Thus, \( T \) is satisfiable if and only if it is consistent.

informal_proof:
To prove the equivalence between satisfiability and consistency, we will demonstrate both directions of the statement.

**Forward Direction (Satisfiability implies Consistency):**
Assume that \( T \) is satisfiable. By definition, this means there exists at least one model that makes all the formulas in \( T \) true simultaneously. If there existed a contradiction within \( T \), it would mean both a formula and its negation are true in that model, which contradicts the existence of such a valid model. Therefore, no contradictions can exist in \( T \), making \( T \) consistent.

**Reverse Direction (Consistency implies Satisfiability):**
Now, assume that \( T \) is consistent. By the definition of consistency, there is no formula from \( T \) such that both it and its negation can be derived from \( T \). This implies that \( T \) is a non-contradictory set of formulas. According to the Completeness Theorem in logic, every consistent set of formulas has a model. Therefore, since \( T \) is consistent, there exists at least one model in which all formulas in \( T \) are true, making \( T \) satisfiable.

Thus, \( T \) is satisfiable if and only if \( T \) is consistent.

Suppose we have a consistent logical theory. By definition, a consistent theory does not contain any contradictions. In model theory, a theory is satisfiable if there exists a model (an interpretation) where all the axioms of the theory are true. 

Since our theory is consistent, it is possible to construct at least one model where all axioms hold true. This is because a consistent theory does not lead to any contradictions, which would make it impossible to have a model. Therefore, the consistency of a theory directly implies its satisfiability.

informal_proof:
Assuming we have a consistent logical theory \( T \), we aim to show that \( T \) is satisfiable. A theory is consistent if and only if it does not contain any contradictions; in other words, there is no sentence \( \phi \) such that both \( \phi \) and \( \neg \phi \) are derivable from \( T \). Similarly, a theory is satisfiable if there exists at least one model where all sentences in \( T \) are true.

The Completeness Theorem in logic establishes that consistency and satisfiability are equivalent. Specifically, if \( T \) is a consistent theory, then there exists a model (a structure that interprets the symbols of the language) where all the sentences of \( T \) are satisfied. Therefore, by the Completeness Theorem, \( T \) must be satisfiable.

informal_statement: For any theory $T$ and formula $\phi$, $\phi$ is true in all models of $T$ if and only if $\phi$ is provable from $T$.
informal_proof:
To establish the equivalence between semantic and syntactic entailment, we consider two directions.

First, assume that $\phi$ is semantically entailed by $T$, i.e., $\phi$ is true in every model of $T$. By the completeness theorem, this implies that $\phi$ is provable from $T$, hence $T \vdash! \phi$.

Second, assume that $\phi$ is provable from $T$, i.e., $T \vdash! \phi$. By the soundness theorem, this entails that $\phi$ is true in all models of $T$.

Thus, we have shown that $\phi$ is semantically entailed by $T$ if and only if $\phi$ is provable from $T$.

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
